name: Cusco & Machu Picchu
tagline: The Inca capital and gateway to Machu Picchu's heights.
bestMonths: Apr, May, Jun, Jul and Aug
whenBlurb: Come in the May-to-September dry season for clear skies and Inti Raymi on June 24; avoid the January-to-March rains, and note the Inca Trail closes all February.

ourTake.lede: Cusco is where you acclimatise before Machu Picchu, so give it two days at altitude before you climb, the mistake everyone makes is rushing straight up. The city itself is a marvel of Inca stonework under Spanish churches; walk San Blas early. Book Machu Picchu and the train weeks ahead, and consider Rainbow Mountain only once your body has adjusted.
ourTake.comeIf: You want Machu Picchu and the Sacred Valley, and you already hold a US or Schengen visa.
ourTake.skipIf: You have limited time, altitude concerns or want a low-effort holiday.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Palacio Nazarenas, A Belmond Hotel
credentials: Belmond (LVMH maison)
Forbes Travel Guide
items.description: A former Inca palace turned convent, now an all-suite Belmond hideaway around a serene courtyard, Cusco's most refined address, with butler service and in-room oxygen.

items.name: Monasterio, A Belmond Hotel
credentials: Belmond (LVMH maison)
Forbes Travel Guide
items.description: A 16th-century monastery beside the cathedral, cloistered courtyards, a 300-year-old cedar and a gilded colonial chapel, the grande dame of Cusco.

items.name: Sanctuary Lodge, A Belmond Hotel
credentials: Belmond (LVMH maison)
items.description: The only hotel at the gates of Machu Picchu, steps from the citadel entrance, letting members walk in at first light before the day crowds arrive.

items.name: JW Marriott El Convento Cusco
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide
JW Marriott (Marriott Luxury)
items.description: A restored 16th-century convent moments from the Plaza de Armas, colonial cloisters, on-site Inca ruins and archaeology, wrapped around full modern luxury.

items.name: Inkaterra La Casona
credentials: Relais & Châteaux
items.description: A 16th-century manor on a quiet plazoleta, Cusco's first Relais & Châteaux, just eleven suites of hand-restored colonial character around a private courtyard.

items.name: Inkaterra Machu Picchu Pueblo Hotel
credentials: Relais & Châteaux
National Geographic Unique Lodges of the World
items.description: Eighty whitewashed casitas in a private cloud-forest reserve by the river below the citadel, the loveliest, most naturalist base for Machu Picchu.

items.name: Explora Valle Sagrado
credentials: Explora (all-inclusive exploration lodges)
Relais & Châteaux (Explora group affiliations)
items.description: An all-inclusive lodge facing the Andes, built for exploration, guided hikes, bikes and Inca sites by day, and a restaurant with a menu shaped by Virgilio Martínez.

items.name: Tambo del Inka, a Luxury Collection Resort & Spa, Valle Sagrado
credentials: The Luxury Collection (Marriott)
Forbes Travel Guide
items.description: A riverside resort in the heart of the valley, the only hotel with its own private station for the train to Machu Picchu, plus a heated indoor pool and spa.

items.name: Sol y Luna, Relais & Châteaux
credentials: Relais & Châteaux
items.description: Casitas scattered across a 37-acre garden estate, hung with contemporary Peruvian art, a characterful, colour-filled Relais & Châteaux in the valley floor.

items.name: Palacio del Inka, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Cusco
credentials: The Luxury Collection (Marriott)
Forbes Travel Guide
items.description: A 500-year-old mansion facing the Koricancha sun temple, grand colonial rooms, a spa and a serious pisco bar, a short walk from the Plaza de Armas.

items.name: Machu Picchu, the Citadel
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu
New7Wonders of the World
items.description: The most famous ruin on earth, and it earns it, a lost Inca city of terraces and temples riding a knife-edge ridge 2,430 metres up, with the green sugarloaf of Huayna Picchu behind and cloud drifting through the valley below. Timed circuit tickets and a licensed guide are now mandatory, so a private advisor books the first entry, the quietest circuit and a guide who paces it gently for grandparents. Arrive by the early train from Ollantaytambo to catch the citadel before the day-trippers.

items.name: Huayna Picchu Climb
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu
items.description: The sheer green peak that towers behind every classic Machu Picchu photograph, a steep, exposed 2 to 3-hour scramble up Inca stairs to temples and terraces perched above the citadel, with a bird's-eye view straight down onto the ruins. Access is capped at a few hundred people a day on a separate timed ticket, so it must be secured months ahead. Not for vertigo or shaky knees; the gentler Machu Picchu Mountain is the multi-gen alternative.

items.name: The Sun Gate (Inti Punku)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu
items.description: The original Inca entrance to the sanctuary, set on a saddle above the citadel where the last day of the Inca Trail delivers trekkers at dawn for their first, breath-catching glimpse of Machu Picchu below. You can walk up to it from the ruins in about an hour and a half without any trek permit, a gentle, rewarding stroll that trades the crowds for silence and one of the great views in the Andes.

items.name: The Classic Inca Trail
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Qhapaq Ñan, Andean Road System
items.description: The pilgrim's road to Machu Picchu, four days over three high passes on original Inca-laid stone, through cloud forest and past ruins invisible from the train, ending at the Sun Gate at first light. Permits are strictly capped, sell out months ahead and cannot be bought day-of; a luxury operator runs it with private porters, a chef and proper tents. High and demanding, for fit travellers, with the one-day Km 104 version for those short on time.

items.name: The Belmond Hiram Bingham Train
items.description: The most glamorous way to reach Machu Picchu, a 1920s Pullman-style luxury train of polished wood and brass with brunch or a four-course dinner, a bar car, live Peruvian music and picture windows onto the Urubamba gorge. Fares run to several hundred dollars each way and include the bus up to the citadel and a guided tour. The effortless, elegant choice for a family who want the journey to feel like part of the treasure.

items.name: The Train from Ollantaytambo
items.description: The workhorse route to Machu Picchu, and a lovely one, glass-roofed carriages from PeruRail and Inca Rail thread the Urubamba river gorge from Ollantaytambo to Aguas Calientes in about ninety minutes. The Vistadome and top-tier Sacred and 360° services add panoramic roofs, snacks and onboard performance. Staying in the Sacred Valley first, then boarding here, is the smart acclimatisation-friendly way to do Machu Picchu without the longer Cusco run.

items.name: Aguas Calientes (Machu Picchu Pueblo)
items.description: The little cloud-forest town at the foot of the mountain where the trains terminate and the buses to the citadel depart, hemmed by jungle peaks and rushing river, with hot springs that give it its name. It is where families overnight to catch the first entry uphill next morning. Belmond's Sanctuary Lodge is the only hotel at the ruins themselves; in town, Inkaterra's cloud-forest reserve is the discreet luxury choice.

items.name: Plaza de Armas
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, City of Cuzco
items.description: The beating heart of the old Inca capital and the finest colonial square in the Andes, arcaded stone balconies, two great churches and a fountain, ringed by peaks and lit gold at night, built directly over the Inca ceremonial plaza of Haucaypata. Sit on a first-floor balcony with a coffee or a pisco sour and watch the city move below. The natural anchor for a first, gentle acclimatisation day before anything strenuous.

items.name: Cusco Cathedral
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, City of Cuzco
items.description: The great Renaissance-Baroque cathedral on the plaza, raised over the Inca palace of Inca Wiracocha and filled with Cusco School canvases, including the famous 'Last Supper' where Christ and the apostles dine on guinea pig and Andean fruit. A private guide unlocks the silver altars, the choir stalls and the black-Christ El Señor de los Temblores, the city's protector. Cool, quiet and unhurried, easy on grandparents.

items.name: Qorikancha (Temple of the Sun / Santo Domingo)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, City of Cuzco
items.description: The holiest temple of the Inca empire, once sheathed in sheets of gold, over which the Spanish built the church and convent of Santo Domingo, so you walk through baroque cloisters and suddenly meet flawless Inca stonework that has survived every earthquake since. No mortar, no gap you could slide paper into; the single clearest lesson in Inca genius in the city. A short, level visit near the centre.

items.name: The Twelve-Angled Stone (Hatun Rumiyoc)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, City of Cuzco
items.description: A single diorite block cut with twelve precise angles to lock seamlessly into the wall of what was an Inca palace and is now the Archbishop's residence, the most photographed stone in Peru, a jeweller's-eye demonstration of masonry without mortar or metal tools. It sits on cobbled Hatun Rumiyoc street a few minutes' walk uphill from the plaza, on the pretty route to San Blas. A quick, delightful stop your guide will point out.

items.name: San Blas Artisan Quarter
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, City of Cuzco
items.description: The bohemian hill quarter above the plaza, steep whitewashed lanes hung with flowers, artists' workshops, silversmiths and the ateliers of Cusco's old carving dynasties, opening onto a small square with a fine viewpoint over the terracotta roofs. The best browsing and the best independent cafés and boutiques in the city. Wander slowly; the altitude bites on the climbs, so let a guide plot a downhill route back to the centre.

items.name: San Pedro Market
items.description: Cusco's great covered food market, under an iron frame attributed to Gustave Eiffel's era, a riot of tropical fruit, cheeses, chocolate, herbs, hanging meat and stalls of fresh juice where locals shop and eat. A cultural feast for curious teenagers and the place to taste your way through the Andes, with plenty of fruit, corn and vegetarian juice bars for meat-free travellers. Go with a guide, keep valuables close, and skip the raw meat aisles.

items.name: Museo Inka
items.description: The city's best museum of the Incas, set in a handsome colonial mansion a block off the plaza, metalwork, mummies, textiles, ceramics and the world's largest collection of queros, the carved wooden ceremonial drinking cups. A calm, well-told introduction that makes the ruins that follow mean far more, and short enough not to tire a multi-generational group. A private curator-led hour turns it into a genuine highlight.

items.name: ChocoMuseo, Bean-to-Bar Workshop
items.description: A charming little chocolate house two blocks from the plaza where children and grandparents alike roast, grind and mould their own bars from Peruvian cacao, and sip Inca-style hot chocolate and cacao-tea. A genuinely fun, hands-on hour for a family with kids, and a warm indoor pause on a cold high-altitude afternoon. Free entry to the shop; the hands-on workshops are booked ahead.

items.name: A Pisco Sour & Andean Coffee Stop
items.description: Cusco takes its coffee and its pisco seriously, single-origin Andean beans roasted in San Blas, and pisco sours shaken at balcony bars over the plaza with the famous frothed egg white and Angostura. A civilised late-afternoon ritual after a day among the ruins, and a way to feel the city's rhythm. Ask for a virgin 'chair de coca' or maracuyá sour and the non-drinkers and children are looked after too.

items.name: Sacsayhuamán
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, City of Cuzco
items.description: The colossal fortress-temple on the hill above Cusco, three tiers of zig-zag ramparts built from limestone blocks, some weighing over 100 tonnes, fitted so tightly the joints defy explanation. It looms over the whole city and hosts the great Inti Raymi sun festival each June. Only a fraction of the original survives, quarried for the colonial city, yet it still astonishes. A private car and guide save the steep climb and bring the stones to life.

items.name: Q'enqo
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, City of Cuzco
items.description: A carved limestone outcrop just past Sacsayhuamán, 'zig-zag' in Quechua, riddled with channels, niches and an underground gallery with a stone altar, once a place of ritual and probably of mummification and sacrifice. Small, strange and atmospheric, easily paired with the other three ruins on the hill above the city in a single morning circuit with a driver. The tunnels and carvings intrigue older children.

items.name: Puka Pukara
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, City of Cuzco
items.description: The 'Red Fort', named for the rosy tint its stone takes at sunset, a compact hilltop complex of terraces, walls and stairways that likely served as a checkpoint or waystation guarding the road into Cusco. It sits right on the Cusco–Pisac road with wide views over the valley, a quick and worthwhile stop on the four-ruins circuit above the city. Best photographed in the late-day light that gives it its name.

items.name: Tambomachay
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, City of Cuzco
items.description: The 'Inca Baths', a beautifully engineered water shrine of stepped terraces, niches and channels fed by a spring that still runs clear through fountains after five centuries, a monument to the Inca reverence for water. It is the highest and gentlest of the four ruins above Cusco, a short level walk from the road. Pair it with Puka Pukara across the way to close a relaxed half-day circuit.

items.name: Pisac Ruins
items.description: One of the Sacred Valley's most spectacular sites, a hilltop Inca town of temples, ritual baths and a sweep of curving agricultural terraces cascading down the mountainside, with the largest known Inca cemetery honeycombing the cliff opposite. Often quieter and even more dramatic than Machu Picchu. A private driver takes you to the upper gate so you can walk gently downhill through the ruins rather than climb.

items.name: Pisac Market
items.description: The famous Andean market spilling across Pisac's plaza and lanes, alpaca knits, silver, ceramics and textiles, busiest and most colourful on Sunday when villagers still come down in traditional dress. The best single place in the valley to shop for gifts, with quality that ranges from tourist trinket to genuine craft, so a guide steers you to the real weavers. Handsome, walkable and a natural pairing with the ruins above.

items.name: Ollantaytambo Fortress
items.description: A towering terraced temple-fortress rising in giant steps above the town, crowned by the unfinished Sun Temple whose six colossal pink-granite monoliths were hauled from a quarry across the valley and up the mountainside, an Inca feat that still baffles engineers. It was the site of one of the few Inca victories over the Spanish. The climb is steep but gradual; a guide sets an easy pace and reveals the stories in the stone.

items.name: Ollantaytambo, the Living Inca Town
items.description: The best-preserved living Inca town anywhere, a grid of cobbled lanes and canchas (walled courtyards) laid out five centuries ago and still inhabited, with water running in the original stone channels down the middle of the streets. Wandering it is the closest you will come to walking through an Inca settlement. It is also the departure point for the Machu Picchu train, so many stay a night in one of its discreet boutique lodges.

items.name: Chinchero, Weaving & the Colonial Church
items.description: A high, traditional village that is the valley's heartland of Andean weaving, where cooperatives demonstrate the whole craft, shearing, washing with soap-root, dyeing with cochineal and plants, and backstrap-loom weaving, and sell textiles of a quality you will not find in the markets. Its adobe colonial church, built on Inca foundations and painted inside, sits above sweeping terraces. A gentle, deeply human stop, and a favourite with families.

items.name: A Weaving Cooperative Visit
items.description: Beyond the demonstrations, community-run cooperatives such as the Center for Traditional Textiles of Cusco keep ancient techniques and natural dyes alive, and a private visit lets you sit with the weavers, see the meaning woven into each pattern and buy directly, with the money staying in the village. A meaningful, unhurried encounter that gives a multi-generational group something real to carry home, and a reason to look closely.

items.name: Moray Terraces
items.description: A set of vast concentric circular terraces sunk into the earth like a green amphitheatre, an Inca agricultural laboratory where the temperature drops several degrees from the top ring to the bottom, letting them test crops across dozens of microclimates. Strange, beautiful and unlike anything else in the valley. A short, easy walk around the rim; a guide explains the ingenious science behind the shapes.

items.name: Maras Salt Pans (Salineras)
items.description: Thousands of small salt terraces cascading down a hillside, fed by a warm salty spring the Incas already worked, still tended by local families who harvest by hand exactly as their ancestors did, a dazzling white-and-ochre mosaic that shifts colour with the sun. Utterly photogenic and easily combined with Moray next door. Take home the pink salt; a private driver links the two in a relaxed half-day.

items.name: Urubamba
items.description: The valley's largest town and its quiet luxury base, lower and warmer than Cusco at around 2,870 metres, which makes it the doctors' choice for acclimatising with older travellers and children before going higher. Around it lie the valley's finest lodges and haciendas, farm-to-table restaurants and horse ranches. Not a sightseeing stop so much as the calm, oxygen-rich heart from which to explore everything else at an easy pace.

items.name: Rainbow Mountain (Vinicunca)
items.description: The mineral-striped ridge that went viral, bands of red, gold, turquoise and lavender laid bare across a 5,036-metre peak, framed by glaciers and grazing alpacas. The reward is huge but so is the altitude: the trailhead alone sits higher than any Alpine summit, so proper acclimatisation and a very early, private start beat the crowds and the afternoon cloud. Horses are available for the final climb; not advised for young children or anyone with heart trouble.

items.name: Palccoyo, the Alternative Rainbow Mountain
items.description: The gentler, quieter answer to Vinicunca, three coloured ridges instead of one, a stone forest and glacier views, reached by a short, nearly flat walk from the road rather than a punishing climb. Far fewer people, and far kinder on the lungs and knees, which makes it the sensible choice for a multi-generational group who still want the rainbow-hills spectacle without the ordeal. Still very high; go slowly and go early.

items.name: Humantay Lake
items.description: A glacier-fed lake of astonishing turquoise cradled beneath the snows of Mount Salkantay at around 4,200 metres, one of the most beautiful day hikes from Cusco, a steep but short climb to a mirror of ice-melt ringed by peaks. The colour has to be seen to be believed. It is high and the ascent is stiff; horses ease the way up, and a private guided day with an early start keeps it calm and safe.

items.name: Tipón
items.description: The Incas' masterpiece of water engineering, a series of grand terraces threaded by stone canals, fountains and channels that still run perfectly, a working monument to their reverence for water and one of the loveliest, least-visited ruins near Cusco. The surrounding village is also famous for slow-roast cuy for those who wish to try it. Quiet, green and easy underfoot, it anchors a rewarding South Valley day away from the crowds.

items.name: Pikillacta
items.description: A rare pre-Inca city, a vast, rigidly gridded settlement of the Wari culture that flourished centuries before the Incas, its high adobe-and-stone walls and hundreds of rooms spread across the plain near the Lucre lake. It gives context most visitors never get: the Andes had great civilisations long before Machu Picchu. Broad and flat to walk, it pairs naturally with Tipón and Andahuaylillas on a South Valley circuit.

items.name: Andahuaylillas, the Sistine Chapel of the Andes
items.description: A modest adobe village church, the Church of San Pedro, that hides one of the most dazzling Baroque interiors in the Americas, every surface painted, a gilded altar, a coffered ceiling and murals so rich it earned its nickname. The plain exterior makes the reveal inside all the more astonishing. The jewel of the South Valley and a serene, level stop for grandparents; combine with Tipón and Pikillacta for a full unhurried day.

items.name: A Despacho Ceremony with an Andean Paqo
items.description: A traditional offering to Pachamama (Mother Earth) and the Apus (mountain spirits), led by a paqo (Andean priest) who builds a mandala of coca leaves, flowers, seeds and symbols to be burned or buried in a rite of gratitude and reciprocity. Arranged privately and respectfully through a good lodge, it is a quiet, moving encounter with a living faith, not a show, and a way for a family to feel the spirit of the mountains they are travelling through.

items.name: Huchuy Qosqo, the Hidden Ruin
items.description: A little-visited Inca royal estate perched on a shelf high above the valley, reached only on foot or horseback, terraces, a great hall and long ramparts with a view straight down to the Urubamba, and usually not another soul in sight. The reward of the hidden gem: Inca grandeur without a turnstile. A guided day-hike or half-day on horseback delivers it; genuinely off the beaten track, so leave it to the acclimatised and able.

items.name: Maras Village & Sky-Kitchen Lunch
items.description: The dusty adobe village above the salt pans has quietly become a stop for exceptional Andean dining, most famously the restaurant of chef Virgilio Martínez's team using produce grown on the valley's own terraces across dozens of altitudes. A meal here is a serious food experience set against big mountain views, and kitchens cater generously to vegetarian and dietary needs on request. A civilised, unexpected pairing with Moray and the salt pans.

items.name: The Cusco School Art Trail
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, City of Cuzco
items.description: Cusco birthed a whole school of colonial painting, Andean artists fusing European religious themes with local colour, gold leaf and hidden Inca symbolism, seen across the Cathedral, the Church of the Society of Jesus on the plaza and the Museo de Arte Religioso. A private art-led morning threads the finest canvases together and reveals the coded resistance in them. Cultured, indoor and gentle, ideal for a rest day between higher exertions.

items.name: San Pedro (Iglesia de la Compañía) & the Plaza Churches
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, City of Cuzco
items.description: The Church of the Society of Jesus (La Compañía) shares the plaza with the Cathedral and rivals it, a soaring Andean-Baroque façade the Jesuits built to outshine their neighbour, over the palace of the Inca Huayna Capac. Climb to the choir balcony for one of the best views over the square. A short, rewarding stop that completes the plaza and shelters you from the midday sun at altitude.

items.name: The Altitude & Acclimatisation Note
items.description: Cusco sits at 3,400 metres and the treks climb far higher, so the single most important piece of planning is time: spend the first day or two low and slow, many advisors put families in the Sacred Valley (around 2,800m) first and save Cusco and Rainbow Mountain for later. Coca tea, gentle pacing, hydration and bottled oxygen help; a doctor's advice on Diamox and any heart condition is essential before the peaks. Plan the itinerary low-to-high, not the reverse.

items.name: MIL
credentials: Latin America's 50 Best Restaurants 2025, No.49
The World's 50 Best Restaurants, 50 Best Discovery
items.description: Virgilio Martínez and Pía León's high-Andes restaurant above the Moray terraces, an eight-course journey through the ecosystems around it, at 3,600 m.

items.name: Cicciolina
credentials: Cusco institution, endorsed by Fodor's, Lonely Planet and the major guidebooks
items.description: A candlelit colonial room above a tapas bar off the Plaza de Armas, Mediterranean technique on Andean produce, and for years the connoisseur's favourite table in Cusco.

items.name: MAP Café
credentials: The World's 50 Best Restaurants, 50 Best Discovery
Set within the Museo de Arte Precolombino (MAP)
items.description: A glass pavilion set in the courtyard of the Pre-Columbian Art Museum, refined, contemporary Peruvian cooking amid one of Cusco's finest collections.

items.name: Chicha por Gastón Acurio
credentials: Gastón Acurio group (Latin America's 50 Best, 50 Best Discovery chef)
items.description: Gastón Acurio's Cusco house on the Plaza Regocijo, regional Andean cooking, from cuy to alpaca and river trout, from Peru's most celebrated chef.

items.name: Uchu Peruvian Steakhouse
credentials: Cusco institution, top-ranked steakhouse, widely guidebook-recommended
items.description: Meats and seafood seared at the table on volcanic hot stones, just off the Plaza de Armas, interactive, generous and a firm Cusco favourite.

items.name: Qespi, JW Marriott El Convento
credentials: Within JW Marriott El Convento (Forbes Travel Guide hotel)
items.description: The elegant dining room of the JW Marriott convent hotel, modern Peruvian cooking with local produce, in colonial-cloister surrounds.

items.name: El Huacatay
credentials: Sacred Valley institution, the valley's top-rated restaurant on the major guides
items.description: A garden restaurant in Urubamba named for the Andean herb, inventive Peruvian-fusion cooking that is the valley's most-loved fine table.

items.name: Kion
credentials: Widely guidebook-recommended, Cusco's leading Chifa
items.description: Cusco's best Chifa, the Peruvian-Cantonese cooking born of Chinese migration, in a warm room near the Plaza Regocijo.

items.name: Kusikuy
credentials: Cusco institution, long-standing traditional favourite
items.description: A long-running family kitchen serving Cusco's classic dishes, the slow-roasted cuy among them, done properly and without ceremony.

items.name: Cicciolina Café
credentials: Under the Cicciolina name, a Cusco institution
items.description: The all-day café arm of Cicciolina, fresh bread, pastries and honest Andean-European plates in a bright, easy room off the main square.

items.name: Museo del Pisco
credentials: Cusco's reference bar for pisco, Peru's national spirit
items.description: A living museum to Peru's national spirit, dozens of piscos and every turn on the pisco sour, with tastings and live music near the Plaza de Armas.

items.name: The Sacred Valley hotel terraces
credentials: Within Tambo del Inka, Sol y Luna and Explora (maison / Relais & Châteaux hotels)
items.description: In the valley, the best evening drinks are the hotel terraces, the fire-lit lounges and pisco bars of the Urubamba resorts, framed by the Andes at dusk.

items.name: Bar Nazarenas, Palacio Nazarenas, A Belmond Hotel
credentials: Within Palacio Nazarenas (Belmond / Forbes Travel Guide)
items.description: The hushed courtyard bar of the Belmond palace-convent, expert pisco sours and Andean cocktails in one of the city's most refined, hidden settings.

items.name: Chicha bar, por Gastón Acurio
credentials: Gastón Acurio group (Latin America's 50 Best, 50 Best Discovery chef)
items.description: The bar of Gastón Acurio's Cusco restaurant on the Plaza Regocijo, Peru's finest chef's take on the pisco sour and Andean-fruit cocktails, before or after dinner.

items.name: Limbus Restobar
credentials: Cusco's landmark rooftop, the city's most celebrated view bar
items.description: An open-air rooftop high in the San Blas quarter with a wall-to-wall panorama over the red roofs of Cusco, the city's signature sundowner and pisco-sour view.

plan.heading: 5 days in Cusco & Machu Picchu, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle into Belmond Palacio Nazarenas, a former convent, and rest for the altitude.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A gentle walk to the Qorikancha sun temple and the San Blas artisan quarter.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: An early, light dinner at MAP Café in the pre-Columbian art museum courtyard.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Plaza de Armas, the cathedral, and the Inca stonework of Hatun Rumiyoc.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Above the city to Sacsayhuamán's great walls in the afternoon light.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Cicciolina or the tasting room at Chicha by Gastón Acurio.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive down to the valley, warmer air, and the salt terraces of Maras and the circles of Moray.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Check into Explora Valle Sagrado or Sol y Luna, then Ollantaytambo's fortress in the low sun.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A quiet dinner at the lodge, resting before the early train.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The first Vistadome train to Aguas Calientes and up to the citadel before the crowds, with a private guide.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at Belmond Sanctuary Lodge at the gate, then a second unhurried pass through the ruins.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return to the valley lodge; a fireside dinner and an early night.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A visit to a Chinchero weaving cooperative for the natural-dye traditions.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Back to Cusco at altitude, one last walk through San Blas.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at Palacio Nazarenas' Senzo before departure.

items.name: San Blas
items.description: The artists' quarter of steep lanes above the centre, atmospheric and quiet.

items.name: Historic centre (Plaza de Armas)
items.description: Around the main square with the cathedral and best hotels, central to everything.

items.name: Sacred Valley (Urubamba/Yucay)
items.description: Lower altitude an hour out, easier on the lungs and closer to the ruins.

events.name: Inti Raymi
events.note: The Inca Festival of the Sun, re-enacted at Sacsayhuamán, the Andes' greatest pageant, fixed on 24 June.

events.name: Corpus Christi
events.note: Saints' processions and feasting fill the Plaza de Armas in the run-up to Inti Raymi.

events.name: Señor de los Temblores (Holy Monday)
events.note: A revered procession of the 'Lord of the Earthquakes' through the old city during Holy Week.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Cusco sits at 3,400m, so sleep first in the lower Sacred Valley (around 2,800m) to soften the altitude, go easy on day one, and take coca tea; secure Machu Picchu entry, a licensed guide and the Hiram Bingham train well in advance as capacity is capped.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Alejandro Velasco Astete (CUZ) from Lima and be met by a private car; many travellers descend the same day to the lower Sacred Valley to acclimatise before Machu Picchu.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver handles Cusco and the Sacred Valley; the final approach to Machu Picchu is the Vistadome or luxury Hiram Bingham train to Aguas Calientes, then a short bus up.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM 4G (Claro, Bitel) is fine in Cusco and the valley but thins out at the ruins; hotel wifi is adequate.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Currency is the Peruvian sol; carry cash for the valley and markets, cards work in Cusco hotels and better restaurants, and tip guides and porters generously.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Dry season May-Sep gives clear skies over Machu Picchu and reliable trekking; the wet season Nov-Mar brings daily rain and cloud, and the Inca Trail closes every February for maintenance.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Reach Peru via Europe (KLM/Amsterdam, Air France/Paris, Iberia/Madrid) into Lima, then a 1h20m LATAM or Sky domestic hop to Cusco; total from India ~28-30h with the connections. Book the Lima-Cusco leg for late morning to clear the frequent early-day mountain weather, and overnight in Lima or the Sacred Valley rather than pushing straight through.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: Cusco sits at ~3,400m, altitude sickness is the real risk; sleep first in the lower Sacred Valley (~2,800m), ascend slowly, and consider acetazolamide after a doctor's advice. No mandatory vaccinations. Bottled water only. The town is safe; the concern here is altitude and pacing, not crime.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian is straightforward, quinoa, potatoes and Andean produce are staples, and Jain is manageable with notice. Indian food is scarce this high up, so plan Indian meals in Lima. Good vegetarian tables exist in central Cusco and at the Sacred Valley lodges.
